title: Burning in microgravity: Experimental results and analysis
summary: Main ISS BRE results paper: 59 successfully ignited 25 mm tests with ethylene/N2 (23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g), 21-40% O2 and 0.56-1 bar, including NASA habitat atmospheres. Over half burned at least 2 and up to 5 minutes; nominal O2 of 26% and above allowed steady flames; shut-down flames were above 94% of steady heat flux; radiative fraction correlated with flame height.

items.quote: More than half of the tests resulted in long burns of at least 2 and as long as 5 min.

items.claim: Nominal O2 of 26% and above allows steady flames.
items.quote: Generally, it has been found that nominal oxygen mole fractions of 26% and above can allow steady flames.

items.claim: Test end points above 94% of steady-state heat flux.
items.quote: Theoretical analyses show the shutdown flames were steady in growth, and all of the test endpoints were more than 94% of steady state in flame heat flux.

items.claim: The analysed tests used two ethylene/N2 mixtures with heats of combustion 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g (LHV), i.e. 50% and 100% ethylene, at 21-40% O2 and 1 to about 0.56 bar, including NASA habitat atmospheres.
items.quote: Mixtures of ethylene and nitrogen allow for 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g heats of combustion (LHV). Nominal ambient conditions range from 40% to 21% oxygen and pressures of 1 to about 0.56 bar. NASA human habitat atmospheres have been used.

notes: Accepted manuscript listed as free on ScienceDirect but refused automated access (HTTP 403); abstract via Semantic Scholar. The 59 tests are the analysed round-1 subset; the PSI table lists 194 flames over all rounds (count difference already in the record's gaps, not a contradiction). The new detail is a test-matrix refinement, not added as a finding.

title: Transient dynamics of radiative extinction in low-momentum microgravity diffusion flames
summary: 3-D simulations of BRE flames in 0 g and 1 g for the orbital test conditions in normal atmosphere (air). Simulated time to extinction agrees with the ISS observations; extinction occurs when the instantaneous radiative fraction reaches 60-70% of the heat release rate, favoured by the long residence time of low-momentum microgravity flames; edge-flame (hook/triple flame) dynamics follow local extinction.

items.claim: Simulated extinction time agrees with ISS observations; extinction occurs when the instantaneous radiative fraction reaches 60-70% of heat release, because of long residence time.
items.quote: Time to flame extinction predicted in this work agrees with the experimental observations. Extinction occurs due to the excessive radiative losses when the instantaneous radiative fraction grows up to 60–70% of the current heat release rate.

items.claim: ISS flames show local extinction, oscillation and complete quenching.
items.quote: The experimental observations have shown that these flames are prone to the local extinction followed by fluctuating instability and complete quenching.

notes: Accepted manuscript listed as free on ScienceDirect but refused automated access; abstract via Semantic Scholar. New finding added to the record.

title: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter
summary: Ground BRE development: emulation of seven condensed fuels (acetone, alcohols, PE, PMMA, PP, PS) with N2-diluted methane, ethylene or propylene, matching heat of combustion, heat of gasification, smoke point and surface temperature; calorimeter accuracy within 5%.

items.quote: Seven condensed fuels were emulated: acetone, ethanol, methanol, polyethylene, polymethylmethacrylate, polypropylene, and polystyrene.

notes: Wiley accepted-manuscript PDF link refused automated access (HTTP 403); abstract via Crossref/Semantic Scholar.

title: Radiative Extinction of Laminar Diffusion Flame above the Flat Porous Burner in Microgravity: A Computational Study
summary: 3-D unsteady simulations replicating BRE (ACME) conditions for methane and ethylene: flames cool by radiation to local extinction, oscillation and extinguishment despite constant fuel supply; microgravity radiative fraction is an order of magnitude higher than at 1 g.

items.claim: Radiative fraction an order of magnitude higher in microgravity; radiative loss causes extinction.
items.quote: The radiative fraction in the microgravity flames is found to be by an order of magnitude higher than that in the normal gravity flames produced by the same burner.

notes: Abstract reconstructed from OpenAlex's word index (as in the record).

title: Transient ellipsoidal combustion model for a porous burner in microgravity
summary: Transient ellipsoidal combustion model of the BRE burner, compared with 5.18 s drop-tower tests where the flame grew ellipsoidally and did not reach steady state.

items.claim: Drop-tower precursor and model; steady state not reached in 5 s.
items.quote: Microgravity BRE experiments conducted at NASA Glenn's 5.18-s Zero Gravity Research Facility indicated the evolution of an approximately ellipsoidal flame moving away from the burner with steady state not achieved during the 5-second test period.

notes: Abstract via Semantic Scholar. Drop tower, not ISS data.

title: Measuring heat flux to a porous burner in microgravity
summary: Calibration of the BRE copper slug calorimeter and comparison with local heat-flux gauges in 5.18 s drop-tower flames; fluxes 5-20 kW/m2 with higher flux at the edge.

items.claim: Drop-tower BRE flames gave burner heat fluxes of 5-20 kW/m2, higher at the burner edge (precursor value, not ISS).
items.quote: The results show that the average slug calorimeter heat flux and the two local heat flux measurements are in harmony over a wide range of microgravity flame fluxes ranging from 5–20 kW/m2, with the edge heat flux much higher.
Microgravity diffusion flames were observed in NASA Glenn's 5.18-s Zero Gravity Research Facility

notes: Abstract via Semantic Scholar. Not added to the record (drop-tower instrument calibration).

title: Analysis of extinction and sustained ignition
summary: Ground (1 g) burner study of sustained ignition and extinction limits with 25-100 mm burners and N2-diluted fuels; critical mass flux ranges about 1-50 g/(m2 s) and no burning below a heat of combustion of 3-4 kJ/g.

items.claim: 1 g limits; no burning below 3-4 kJ/g heat of combustion.
items.quote: The results show that no burning is possible below a heat of combustion of 3–4 kJ/g.

notes: Full abstract from the Lund University research portal (Semantic Scholar's copy is truncated).

title: A Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) for study of condensed fuel burning in microgravity
summary: 49 BRE drop-tower tests (25 and 50 mm; methane, ethylene, diluted ethylene): flames nearly hemispherical within 5 s and still growing; larger burner lacks correlation, attributed to gas radiation; quasi-steady microgravity flames need much longer than 5 s.

items.claim: Quasi-steady microgravity BRE flames need much longer than 5 s (why ISS tests were needed).
items.quote: The analysis predicts that quasi-steady microgravity BRE flames will require much longer than 5 s.
This paper presents 49 BRE tests at NASA Glenn's 5.18-s Zero Gravity Research Facility for two burner diameters (25 mm and 50 mm) with methane, ethylene and nitrogen-diluted ethylene as fuels.
